items.excerpt: Gholam-Hossein Sa’edi’s The Mourners of Bayal (1964) remains one of the defining works of modern Iranian literature. items.body: Gholam-Hossein Sa’edi’s The Mourners of Bayal (1964) remains one of the defining works of modern Iranian literature. Across eight interconnected stories set in the fictional village of Bayal, Sa’edi explores poverty, famine, superstition, grief and death through a world where collective anxiety gradually erodes the distinction between reality and hallucination. Equally striking is his attention to sound. The village first announces itself acoustically: dogs bark across rooftops, a bell drifts through the darkness, voices pass from window to window, footsteps punctuate long stretches of silence. Bayal is heard before it is fully seen. Tegh & Adel Poursamadi respond directly to this sonic imagination, drawing not on the individual plots of the stories but on their atmosphere and, above all, on the way Sa’edi constructs the village through listening as much as through sight. Like Ima and After You Left, Bayal بیل grew out of extended improvisational dialogues between Tegh’s electronics and Adel Poursamadi’s violin, viola and traditional Iranian instruments before being carefully sculpted into finished compositions. Yet this third collaboration feels markedly more concentrated than its predecessors. The earlier records moved through broader dynamic contrasts, opening onto expansive drones. Bayal بیل occupies a narrower emotional register, maintaining an almost continuous state of subdued tension lending the album a quiet claustrophobia entirely in keeping with Sa’edi’s village, where lives unfold beneath the weight of forces that remain largely unseen. The opening “Black Stone” establishes that landscape from the outset. Electronics and bowed strings emerge from a dense greyscale haze where instrumental identities remain deliberately obscured. Sounds appear like distant outlines. “The Cow” deepens this sense of collective but undefined presence. Throughout the piece, faint layers of indistinct voices drift through the mix like fragments of overheard conversation, suggesting the murmur of Bayal’s unseen inhabitants as they move through alleys and courtyards beyond the listener’s field of perception. These ghostly traces repeatedly dissolve into silence before returning once more, punctuated by resonant strikes that resemble a ritual gong, briefly gathering the surrounding sounds before allowing them to disperse again. The effect closely recalls Sa’edi’s opening pages, where barking dogs, distant bells and whispered exchanges establish the village long before individual characters emerge. “Toward the Vast Mountain” broadens the perspective without abandoning the prevailing sense of enclosure. Percussive markers recur throughout the piece, functioning almost like ritual or processional signals that quietly propel the music forward through its suspended atmosphere. The composition advances with measured inevitability, each percussive gesture subtly reorienting the listener while strings dissolve into electronic residue. “Pāpākh” is the shortest track on the album and refers to the village dog in Sa’edi’s stories, whose barking, pacing and sudden silences are interpreted by Bayal’s deeply superstitious inhabitants as signs of looming disaster. The music mirrors that heightened state of alertness without becoming illustrative. “Zanguleh” occupies a distinctive place within the album. Whereas much of Bayal treats the strings as part of a larger electroacoustic fabric, here Adel Poursamadi’s playing comes decisively to the foreground. Long, lyrical violin lines unfold over a restrained electronic backdrop whose role is less to obscure than to sustain the instrument’s resonance. The piece carries the emotional weight of a lament, offering the album’s clearest expression of grief without disturbing its overall restraint. After the denser first half, its relative transparency feels almost startling. The closing “Under the Willow Tree” follows naturally, letting suspended harmonics, slowly decaying resonance and carefully measured silences carry the emotional weight long after the final sounds have disappeared. The artwork by Atoosa Pourhosseini extends this vision with remarkable coherence. Anonymous figures occupy the margins of a blurred architectural landscape whose contours dissolve beneath mist, grain and diffuse light. The image perfectly reflects Tegh’s description in the liner notes of approaching Sa’edi’s village from the crest of a hill, where movements remain visible but faces, conversations and individual lives disappear into distance. Like the music itself, it withholds detail in favour of atmosphere, inviting the viewer to contemplate Bayal from the same remove that shapes the album’s entire aesthetic. The affinity between Sa’edi’s prose and Tegh and Poursamadi’s music extends beyond mood. The Mourners of Bayal rarely explains events directly, allowing rumour, fragments of dialogue and sensory details to shape the reader’s understanding. Bayal follows the same logic. Voices remain indistinct, instrumental identities blur, and meaning accumulates through resonance, silence and suggestion rather than narrative illustration. Slow, and foreboding, the album faithfully captures the psychological climate of Sa’edi’s fictional village, translating one of the great works of Iranian literature into an electroacoustic language of emotional depth. photo by Aram Tahmasebi To find out more we reached out directly to Tegh and Poursamadi. Unfortuantely, due to the current situation in Iran, only Tegh was available to answer. Ima ایما imagined post-human communication through a dialogue between acoustic instruments, Iranian traditional music and electronics, while After You Left revolved around memory and uncertainty. With Bayal, the starting point is much more concrete: Gholam-Hossein Sa’edi’s The Mourners of Bayal. Yet the new album also feels more restrained and claustrophobic than the previous two, remaining within a remarkably narrow emotional and dynamic range. Did the world of Sa’edi’s book lead you towards this concentration, or was this already a direction your musical dialogue was taking after After You Left? TEGH: Yes, exactly. The atmosphere of the book had a very strong influence on the sound of the album. IMA was supposed to be the first chapter of a larger project. The idea was to continue the project by working with other musicians from different backgrounds and bring different worldviews into the kind of world-building I had in mind. Unfortunately, this part of the project has not really worked out so far. But after the first album, both of us wanted to continue working together. We wanted to keep the colours, contrasts and freedom that we found in the making of IMA, but develop them further and make them more mature. We felt that this could give us a lot of potential for different kinds of experiments, both in terms of meaning and technique. This led to After You Left, and I think it will also be present in some of the work we release in the future. But Bayal follows a different path. I see it as a completely different chapter. As you said, the album stays within the space it presents initially, and to me, the pieces have very simple forms of storytelling, and these qualities came from our personal reading of the atmosphere of the book. In The Mourners of Bayal, it was not so much the events themselves that affected us, but the atmosphere of the book. I feel that this atmosphere does not change very much throughout the book and stays with you. The political and social uncertainty in the stories, the way everything is unreal and yet it becomes believable, and the fact that the stories seem to be made up of people who feel isolated from each other, maybe strangers to one another, and sometimes even strangers to themselves, all affected us. This idea of alienation is present throughout the book. Even in that small fictional village, society itself can hurt and oppress people. The village is surrounded by poverty, death, illness and hunger. All of these things pushed us towards creating a more claustrophobic and oppressive atmosphere in the album. Maybe “post-defeat” is the right word for it. That is my own personal way of describing it. What struck me while reading The Mourners of Bayal is how much of the village Sa’edi constructs through sound: barking dogs, bells, footsteps, voices travelling between houses, and long stretches of silence often precede any clear understanding of what is happening. Your description of approaching Bayal “from the top of a hill”, hearing cries and other sounds without being able to make out their details, seems closely related to this. Were you consciously responding to Sa’edi’s use of sound and listening as literary devices, and how did you translate that sense of hearing a community at a distance into pieces such as “The Cow” and “Pāpākh”? TEGH: I think that is exactly spot on. Sa’edi’s use of sounds, and the way he created the atmosphere of the book through them, was one of the reasons we chose this specific work. It was not really a conscious decision to respond to this aspect of the book. We never really sat down and talked about choosing this direction. I think we were simply influenced by it to such an extent that it found its way into the album naturally. For example, there is the sound of the bell attached to the empty carriage, coming from far away in the desert. It is mentioned several times throughout the book, often in connection with moments where there is death. The character of this sound, and the meaning it carries, had a strong effect on us and led us towards making “Zanguleh,” which means “bell” in Farsi. It might sound strange or unrelated, but this carriage and its bell also remind me of the cart in Béla Tarr’s The Turin Horse. It creates a very heavy image like that in my mind. The idea of looking at the events from a distance, as if we were standing on top of a hill looking at the village, came from our wish not to create a direct sonic retelling of the book. This perspective allowed us to stay away from simply recreating the events and focus more on what we personally felt from the atmosphere of the book and do our own thing based on that. We wanted to make music based on the effect the book had on both of us, rather than trying to represent the story itself. That is also why we left quite a lot of time between reading the book and starting to make the music. We wanted to forget as many details of the stories as possible and work only with what had remained in our minds, and of course it helped us avoid using the sounds from the book in a more literal way. For example, Papākh, the village dog, is one of the most important characters in the book for me. He has a strong presence, and in a way he observes everything while remaining silent and the villagers have a strange relationship with him. In general, the villagers have very close relationships with animals. The relationship between Mashdi Hassan and his cow, Islam and his goat, Papākh and the villagers, all stayed in my mind. The fact that this is a village suffering from famine, where some people have to go from one village to another to beg or steal food, but they still do not kill their animals for food, was particularly striking to me. The two tracks came out of this. We were more interested in making music out of the feeling we got from the presence of these characters in the story, rather than directly referring to the sound of Papākh or Mashdi Hassan’s cow. You describe the recording process as a series of improvisational dialogues that were subsequently processed and structured, with responding to the concept taking precedence over conventional musical rules. From your perspective, how does that process work? When Adel produces a sound, are you responding to it electronically in real time, or do the more radical transformations happen later during editing and processing? And at what point, for you, does an improvisation cease to be the documentation of a performance and become a composed piece? TEGH: Naturally, this way of working was not something new for Adel and me. We worked in an almost similar way on the two previous albums as well. We talked a lot about the effect the atmosphere of the book had on us. We both knew what elements of it made us hear things, and what kind of feelings we wanted to communicate. But we never really talked about what the tracks should sound like, what their structure should be, or what we should or should not do. The process usually started with one of us doing something, and the other responding to it. This would continue through different sessions, and then we would listen back to the recordings. Sometimes, from a one-hour recording, only one melody and one beat would come out, like in “Toward the Vast Mountain.” We felt that they were close to the concept we had in mind, and then we developed them into a track at a later stage. “Zanguleh” and “The Black Stone,” for example, both came out of the recording of a single session. A lot of the changes and processing happened afterwards, especially the processing of the sounds and shaping the forms. This was important for bringing the different sounds together and making them feel like they belonged to the same world. One of the main reasons for this is that I am honestly not a very good improviser. In many of the sessions, instead of being able to immediately reach the sound I had in mind, I was more often just leaving some kind of indication of what I wanted to reach later. For example going back to “Toward the Vast Mountain,” I had already written a beat for the melody in the improvisation, but the sounds and the pattern were quite different from what you hear on the final track. As for the last part of your question, it is a little difficult to explain. There is a point during the process when you suddenly think, “Ah, we found it. This is becoming something.” It is a moment when you find each other, everything starts to work together, and you feel that you have reached something. For me, that is the point where I can change the way I look at the material. I can stop thinking only about finding sounds or making the improvisation work, and start looking at what we have from the perspective of storytelling and how the idea can develop, where it can go, and how it can become a composition. artwork by Atoosa Pour Hosseini One of the most affecting moments for me is “Zanguleh”, because Adel’s violin suddenly becomes much more exposed and lyrical after spending much of the record partially submerged within the electroacoustic texture; it almost functions as a lament before “Under the Willow Tree” carries the record towards silence. Across Ima ایما , After You Left and now Bayal بیل, has your understanding of the relationship between strings and electronics changed? Are you increasingly interested in making it difficult to tell where one ends and the other begins, and what made you choose to break that ambiguity so strikingly on “Zanguleh”? TEGH: Absolutely. One of the things I personally question now after several years of working with Adel is exactly this. In IMA, and to some extent in After You Left, there is still quite a clear distance between the sound of the instruments and the electronics. Maybe you could say that the meeting between my world and Adel’s world did not always become a third world, something that was neither completely mine nor completely his. I think this improved in After You Left, and we got even closer to it with Bayal. I would not necessarily say that I am trying to make it difficult to tell the sounds apart. What is more important to me is that, in the composition, sound design and all the different stages of the process, I do not treat the instruments and electronics as separate things. I also try not to let the source of a sound decide how I treat it. I want to reach a point where by the end of the process there is a kind of continuity between the sounds, and they feel like they belong to the same family. It does not matter whether you can recognise where each sound comes from, what matters is that when these different sonic characters are put together, they do not feel like they have been taken from completely different worlds and simply placed next to each other like a collage. As for “Zanguleh,” as I mentioned earlier, the track was influenced by the sound of the bell coming from far away in the story. In my personal interpretation, I connect this sound with death, not as an ending, but as something that has been staying with you. As you said, that section was meant to work almost like a lament. It is actually a mourning. Our idea was for the track to reach a point where it could finally break out and mourn freely, and that is where the track ended up. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 专辑改编自伊朗现代文学经典，回应原作中以声音构建村庄的听觉叙事。Tegh 的电子声响与 Adel Poursamadi 的小提琴、中提琴及伊朗传统乐器经长期即兴对话后精心雕琢成型，呈现出比前作更为凝聚的情绪张力。电子与拉弦乐器从浓密灰阶迷雾中浮现，个体音色被刻意模糊，远方隐约人声与回响击奏构成村庄幽灵般的存在痕迹。全作维持一种低伏不安的压抑氛围，营造出与原作村落相呼应的幽闭感，将伊朗文学的听觉想象转化为当代实验声响景观。

items.body: Felice Sciorilli first graced our pages last spring, appearing on Biodiversità Records’ 14 Soundcapes with the track “Breaths.” At the time, we recognized the unique nature of the piece, capturing the sound of “air pushed through the Etruscan sandstone cliffs by the incoming waves.” “Breaths” appears on Distant Places as well, a worthy inclusion. In a way, the album title is a misnomer. These places are not necessarily geographically distant; most come from the intertidal zone of the Tyrrhenian Sea. But as Sciorilli has a particular fascination with tide pools – some only centimeters deep – these sounds may be regarded as distant as most people seldom if ever encounter their nuances. When one hears that an album is recorded at the coast, one expects to hear a bevy of predictable material: wind and waves, gulls and other fair-weather fowls. These make appearances, but are not primary. Instead, Sciorilli concentrates on micro-sounds made macro. In “E,” water rushes into crevasses before spurting back out, powered by the force of the waves, although this is not technically the sound of the waves. Instead, this is the sound of waves in rocks, familiar to jetty walkers. As the angles of approach vary, so do the timbres. The tide pools first come into focus in the opening segment of “Cluster,” with a sound akin to the crackle of brine shrimp. The piece develops in movements, like the “Bohemian Rhapsody” of field recording. Soon there are crashing waves, then fizzes and pops, and finally the sound of pebbles tossing, turning, rolling back to the sea. “Bolle” and “Bubbles drift upward into the water” occupy different areas of the album while also being separated by tone. While hearing them, one recalls pablo diserens’ “The Shrinking Glacier” from last year’s ebbing ice lines, providing one with the opportunity to compare “healthy” bubbles with “unhealthy” bubbles, or bubbles that belong to a cycle with those escaping for the last time. The second piece is more effervescent, like alien birds swimming in soda; without hydrophones, one might never encounter such distant sounds. While listening, one is amazed by the number of musical parallels that can be found in nature: the quickening tempos of “From the Tidal Edge,” the glissandos of “Outflow.” Distant Places serves as a reminder that music imitates nature, not (save for starlings) the other way around. The set builds to the eighteen-minute centerpiece “Tiny Worlds,” a longer, reworked version of a piece that made the shortlist of The Radiophonic Broadcast’s Sounds of the Year 2025-26. Recorded in a tidal pool six centimeters deep (shown in the pdf that accompanies the download), the piece demonstrates just how rich, dense and diverse a micro-world can be, although to be fair, to the local Littorina snails there also exist micro-worlds within micro-worlds, from bacteria down to the smallest atom, each with a corresponding biophony. The “characters” that appear may be animate or inanimate, but each possesses a personality of its own: squeaking and whistling, popping and percolating. In the final piece, Sciorilli draws back from the water and embeds his microphone in the sand, muffling the sound of the nearby waves. “Under the Sand” operates as a parable. Sonic treasures are available everywhere, yet most of us never hear them; it is as if we too are buried in the sand, listening through wax and debris, treating micro-worlds as distant places although they are right beneath our feet. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: field recording / ambient / experimental / sound art
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以田野录音为核心方法，将意大利第勒尼安海潮间带的微观声响转化为音乐素材。Sciorilli并不依赖风浪与海鸥等可预期的海岸声音，而是聚焦于潮池中几厘米深的微型世界：水流涌入石缝又喷涌而出的声音、卤虫的细碎声响、气泡在水中的上升轨迹、鹅卵石翻滚归海的摩擦。所有这些通过水听器捕捉的声响被放大、编排，形成具有乐句结构与运动发展逻辑的声景作品。专辑中的乐曲展现出与自然界高度吻合的音乐性：渐快的节奏变化、滑音式的水流运动、密集而层次分明的织体。十八分钟的核心曲目在六厘米深的潮池中录制，证明了即使在最微小的水域环境中，也能呈现出极为丰富、多样且密集的声学景观。整张专辑既是对自然声响的忠实记录，也是一种以田野录音为媒介的作曲实践。

items.body: Review by Logan — There is a distinct emotional friction at the core of Music Has the Right to Children. The albumtriggers a strong sense of nostalgia in me, but it rarely feels entirely safe or comforting. Instead, my own experience with the record lands in a bittersweet, haunted territory where thedegraded educational samples and childhood imagery evoke memories that feel slightly wrong ordisplaced. When I listen to it, the music operates like a half-forgotten television broadcast fromyouth left to rot on a discarded VHS tape.A significant reason this atmosphere connects with me is the physical groove of the record. Unlikethe colder, more mechanical programming of their later electronic peers, the rhythm section herestrikes me as dusty and organic. My personal standout of this approach is "Aquarius". The trackanchors its counting-game vocal samples with a heavy, driving bassline and a hip-hop breakbeat thatcommands the room. To me, it represents the clear peak of the duo's ability to blend a functionalrhythmic pocket with an unsettling psychological undertone.That rhythmic focus carries right through what I consider the rest of the album's essentialhighlights. The deliberate, motorik propulsion of "Happy Cycling" provides a steady late-albumsurge, while the texturally complex beat on "An Eagle in Your Mind" showcases their mastery ofanalog tape manipulation. Even on a short, melodic pop vignette like "Roygbiv", which could easilyslide into saccharine territory, I find that the underlying groove ensures the track never dissolvesinto pure sentimentality. The brothers keep the entire project grounded in a heavy, physicalreality that I find myself returning to.The technical blueprint of the album confirms that this texture was never an accident. The Sandisonbrothers achieved this frayed quality through a deliberate process of analog degradation, treatingtheir studio like a laboratory for decaying magnetic tape. Instead of relying on the digitalprecision of late-nineties sequencing, the duo ran their synthesizers?frequently utilising the warm,unstable sub-bass of the Roland SH-101 and the gritty digital-to-analog character of the EnsoniqVFX-SD directly into decrepit tape machines. By bouncing audio onto consumer-grade Tascam four-track recorders and malfunctioning Grundig decks, they subjected clean melodies to physical wow-and-flutter, artificial dropouts, and tape saturation.This destructive production method transforms standard subtractive synthesis into a tactileexperience. On tracks like "An Eagle in Your Mind", the skittering rhythm section and heavilywarped vocal elements sound to my ears as though they are actively dissolving under the friction ofa sticking tape head. Similarly, the low-end thunk and swirling synths of "Aquarius" owe theirpresence to low bit-depth Akai S1000 samplers, which naturally crush the high frequencies and add adistinctive, dusty grit to the breakbeat. By leaning into the unpredictable quirks of old gearrather than flawless digital tracks, the duo built a soundscape where everything feels beautifullydecayed, matching how human memory blurs over time.This focus on unstable analog hardware explains why simpler pop vignettes like "Roygbiv" still hitme so hard. The track is built on a remarkably straightforward melodic hook, but the underlyingproduction ensures it never sounds cheap or overly sweet. The bassline carries a heavy, physicalthrum that balances out the drifting, sun-baked top melodies, proving to me that the duo could writean infectious pop tune without losing their signature sonic grit. It functions as my personalgateway into the album's stranger, more texturally complex spaces.By the time the record reaches "Happy Cycling", that playful energy has mutated into something farmore relentless. The track acts as a steady late-album surge, driving forward on a cyclical,motorik rhythm that feels both hypnotic and slightly ominous. The repetition does not tire me out;instead, it locks you into a specific, heavy-limbed trance that mirrors the physical exhaustion of along journey. By placing this sprawling, rhythmic marathon near the end of the tracklist, theSandison brothers solidify the album's broader structural arc, ensuring the listener finishes theexperience immersed in their strange, loop-based universe.Looking back at this debut from the vantage point of their broader discography reveals just howcrucial these early structural blueprints were. Music Has the Right to Children acted as thefoundational source code for every sonic mutation that followed across the next three decades. Thewarm, electro-acoustic infrastructure and acoustic guitar textures that defined The CampfireHeadphase find their genetic origin here in the brief, pastoral transitions of "The Color of theFire" and "Olson". The duo was already learning how to weaponise nostalgia, laying the groundworkfor a lighter, more organic detour before their mid-career pivot.Concurrently, the album contains the initial seeds of the cold, apocalyptic dread that eventuallyswallowed Tomorrow's Harvest and Inferno. The unsettling vocal mutations on "An Eagle in Your Mind"and the eerie, numeric counting games of "Aquarius" are early warning signs of the claustrophobic,paranoid environments that defined their later records. By balancing infectious hip-hop groovesagainst a deeply haunted psychological undertone, Music Has the Right to Children did not justlaunch the Sandison brothers' career; it established a timeless tension that they would spend thenext thirty years refining, dismantling, and rebuilding.Ultimately, Music Has the Right to Children remains a significant achievement because it refuses toage. While the late-nineties electronic scene largely chased hyper-polished digital futures, Boardsof Canada looked backward, constructing a sonic monument out of decaying magnetic tape andfragmented childhood ghosts. It is a record that demands you surrender your internal clock and sitwith the discomfort of its bittersweet, haunted landscapes. Nearly three decades after its release,its physical grooves and emotional friction continue to command authority, standing for me as thedefinitive masterpiece of a discography that has yet to be replicated.While I do consider this album to be a masterpiece, "Aquarius" in particular remains one of myfavourite Boards of Canada tracks, and this was one of my very favourite albums for years, aftergetting Inferno this does not appeal to me as much. Music has the Right to Children and Geogaddiwere my favourite BoC albums, but now those final three mean more to me. So this masterpiece willget a 4 at PA (I would go with 4.5 if we had the option as I did at RYM). Additionally, I primarily wanted to add BoC to Prog Archives for the final three albums.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It is always good to blend humor with strong influences, and right from the opening track of their debut album, "Lambo No. 5," a play on the famous "Mambo", Rokost draws on inspirations ranging from Dave Douglas and his "ethnic" trumpet style to Miles Davis and the use of special effects to create unique sonic textures. At times, the music seems to venture into psychedelic territory without ever losing its infectious, frenetic rhythm. Later, Marta Winnitzki's Rhodes piano (she also plays synthesizers) introduces mid-tempo passages that shift the rhythm, though the original melody, driven by Michel Schroeder's trumpet, always returns. This Hamburg-based quartet plays with time signatures and reimagines them; we recognize the conventions of classic jazz-rock while sensing them being pushed beyond their limits, not to abandon the genre, but to "expand the battlefield," to borrow a phrase from Michel Houellebecq.Menschenfeind evokes a space-age atmosphere, yet in its own unique way, distinct from the past, though nods to that era remain. Synthesizers dart back and forth reminiscent of the 70s, while the trumpet and keyboards establish a more contemporary setting where the two elements collide. This is where the term "symphonic jazz" applies, not due to pomp or grandiosity, but because of the interplay between the keyboards and the bass-and-trumpet foundation, with the latter instruments taking their own solos."Trotz" is dissonant and syncopated until a driving rhythm, so electric it borders on electronic, builds in intensity; its staccato breaks are slightly reminiscent of Bill Bruford's Earthworks. At times, one gets the impression that if Miles Davis were still with us, he might be creating something akin to the track "Jazon Hunter Strikes Again!"; much like the brilliant Japanese pianist Hiromi Uehara, her admiration for the 1970s drives a fusion of contemporary avant-garde with classic progressive elements, dreamy synthesizers, sophisticated trumpet lines, and a floating groove. Here, the sounds of the 70s, 80s, and 90s, along with techno, blend into a pastiche that serves as both homage and a gateway to the dreamlike "Meloda," a piece where electronic music once again takes on a progressive character within a jazz context."Attitude Adjustment" has a full-on rock rhythm, guitars aren't needed; as Weather Report so aptly demonstrated, the timing comes from elsewhere. A distorted synthesizer creates just the right kind of confusion to scramble the senses, while the bass and drums hammer out their parts, underpinning solos that scale mountains and swim through rivers, pumping adrenaline into those greens and fruits, produce as organic as this musical concept itself, where the artificial element pulses with more life than ever."We Will Still Be Here Tomorrow" is split in two; a classical trumpet shifts into a Baroque style while something very modern emerges from the seemingly disjointed drum beats. Yet, just when there might be a moment of coherence and composure, "Lines & Crimes" introduces a disorder that nonetheless encompasses melody and meaning, for this instrumental music seems to tell a story. The keyboards go wild, while the trumpet wails in increasingly piercing, high-pitched tones. "The Machines That Walk At Midnight" is almost industrial in its mechanical rhythm, yet there is genuine feeling when the bass kicks in; the electronic element has permeated not just the sound but the composition itself. Amidst this, Michel Schroeder adds a warm, magical touch on the trumpet, playing with effortless class and style, to remind us that this spirit doesn't subtract or lose anything, but rather adds to and elevates the music.Continuing the metaphor linking Rokost's music to Houellebecq's literature, one could say that the elementary particles of the fusion are present here but developing independently; they continue to evolve, triggering the release of substances like serotonin, the neurotransmitter that relays messages between nerve cells and helps regulate various bodily functions.The map and the territory are already laid out on the table, exposed; now it is simply a matter of submission to the possibility of an island... where all these molecules arrive and rearrange themselves, ultimately altering matter.

items.body: This new album by Alessandro Tedeschi—better known by his sonic alter ego, Netherworld—is a remarkable work. Quite by chance, thanks to his young daughter, he stumbled upon old recordings dating back more than twenty years. These were recordings he had all but forgotten. Upon rediscovering them and realizing that their atmosphere perfectly matched the dark, sombre period he had been going through in recent months, he decided to revisit and rework material that no one had ever heard before. You could quite rightly call these Netherworld’s earliest experiments. Seven tracks were salvaged and restored. They fit seamlessly into the concept of Glacial Movements—Alessandro’s own label—leaving a profound, icy impression through their Ambient and Cinematic sound. We discover a Soundscape created—and, above all, inspired—by early expeditions to the North Pole. Distinctive field recordings echo through the metallic tones. You sense the imaginary presence of malevolent forces watching you, potentially pushing you towards a state of paranoia; you experience a sense of evil and an invisible presence that relentlessly pursues you. This effect is achieved simply through the power of the compositions, which, in my opinion, might well be hailed as Netherworld’s finest work. The sound is authentic and archaic, with deep, dominating tones that hit their mark with undeniable impact. It is hardly surprising, then, that the only track that failed to fully captivate me was the most ethereal one on the album. When music becomes an expression of dark thoughts, an artist is often at their most inspired—a fact perfectly embodied by the evocative title, “The Hermit”. (Rating:8). Listen to “Loneliness”: Loneliness by Netherworld About Netherworld Netherworld is the moniker of Alessandro Tedeschi, an Italian ambient and dark ambient composer based in Rome. The project is released through Tedeschi’s own label Glacial Movements, which he founded in 2006; “The Hermit” marks the label’s 20th anniversary. Netherworld’s music draws on manipulated fragments of classical music and field recordings, including ice masses, aurora-related material and Arctic wind recordings. Before focusing on Glacial Movements, the project released music through labels including Fario, Angle Rec, Umbra and Taalem. “Eternal Frost”, recorded in 2004, was originally issued by Umbra in a hand-numbered edition of 99 copies and later appeared on Bandcamp in February 2022. The Glacial Movements catalogue includes “Mørketid” (2007), “Over The Summit” (2011) and “Alchemy Of Ice” (2013, Tedeschi’s tenth full-length release). In 2017, Netherworld collaborated with Eraldo Bernocchi on “Himuro” for the label’s Iceberg Series. “Algida Bellezza” followed in 2019, and Side-Line’s interview with Netherworld was built around that release. “Vanishing Lands” appeared in 2022 and the Bvdub collaboration “Equilibrium” in 2023. “The Hermit” returns to material recorded before Glacial Movements existed: seven tracks salvaged from deteriorated CD-Rs and Minidiscs recorded in 2004.
items._genre: dark ambient / ambient / cinematic / field recording
items._cn_summary: 意大利作曲家Netherworld（Alessandro Tedeschi）偶然从女儿处发现二十余年前的旧录音，这些早于其厂牌Glacial Movements成立的实验性素材被重新混音修复，构成专辑《The Hermit》。整张作品以北极探险为意象基底，将金属质感的合成器音色与冰原、极光、极地风声的田野录音相融合，营造出辽远而阴郁的氛围空间。作曲手法偏重纯器乐与声响设计，七首曲目层层推进，在暗色调的音景中嵌入一种被无形力量注视与追踪的不安感。乐评认为这是其创作生涯中最为出色的作品之一，深沉的支配性音色具有强烈感染力，仅最缥缈空灵的一首稍欠力度。专辑同时作为厂牌二十周年的纪念之作，展现了艺术家在暗潮与环境音乐交叉领域的长线探索脉络。

items.body: So much has been written about John Coltrane and he's such a widely acknowledged and worshiped figure - one of jazz's top two most iconic artists, along with his once employer Miles Davis - that I don't feel I have anything new to bring to the table. Asked to comment on a favorite Coltrane album, however, I comply, for what it's worth. The first Coltrane album I purchased - a secondhand 1987 CD release - was Live at the Village Vanguard Again , recorded May 28, 1966. Prior to this, I had only heard Coltrane on Miles Davis' Kind of Blue . Village Vanguard Again was a punch in the gut, a puzzle for the mind and the record that won me over to free jazz for good, although it didn't happen overnight. I initially didn't understand what was going on, what to make of it. But was soon repeatedly attracted by the unhinged, torrential sounds unleashed on lengthy versions of "Naima" (a tender ballad with exquisite chords, here exuding rage and sorrow) and "My Favorite Things" (a distinctly lighthearted song from the movie "The Sound of Music", here given a terminally outrageous, or wonderfully out there treatment, according to your inclinations) interspersed with a six-minutes Jimmy Garrison bass solo. Each time I pressed the play button, I was unable to stop listening until the end of the total running time. The album held some arcane truth I couldn't live without anymore. It was music I had to sort out for myself, keep to myself, not music I could share with friends or relatives, let alone spin at parties... The line up had Alice Coltrane on piano, Pharoah Sanders on tenor sax and flute, Rashied Ali on drums, with Coltrane on tenor, soprano and bass clarinet. I was unaware there was a much-loved Coltrane "classic quartet" then, and that this was not it! Some of the Impulse! catalogue was being reissued at that time (the mid-90s), Sanders' "Tauhid" and "Karma" among the batch, both also expanding my musical outlook. Coltrane's albums and archival releases were dropping in quick succession, each new one a mandatory listen. I stumbled on small-priced, worn out LP copies of "Transition" and "Kulu Se Mama" (both recorded in 1965). I was hooked, although none of those albums, and no other Coltrane record I heard after the 1966 live set, had the same definitive, life-altering effect, or reached the same high as that first exposure to the work. Could it be that I had started with a peak, a logical conclusion to what had come before? The music was equal parts perplexing, intimidating, meaningful, dark, luminous, an unrelenting war machine yet brimming with sensitivity, not quite inviting if you were not ready to surrender to its revolutionary approach, but fully uplifting and cleansing if you were. items._genre: free jazz / avant-garde / spiritual jazz / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这张1966年Village Vanguard现场录音是Coltrane晚期探索的代表作，阵容包括Alice Coltrane钢琴、Pharoah Sanders次中音萨克斯与长笛、Rashied Ali鼓手以及Coltrane本人演奏次中音、高音与低音单簧管。评论者回忆初次聆听时被其猛烈而难以理解的音响所冲击，但反复聆听后逐渐被那段失控般的洪流之声所俘获——Naima从柔美抒情被改写为愤怒与悲怆，My Favorite Things则从轻快电影歌曲化为极度狂野的即兴重构，Jimmy Garrison的六分钟低音独奏穿插其间。评论者认为这张专辑对他而言是改变人生的转折点，将其引向自由爵士领域，并指出Coltrane这一时期的作品如同不可分享的私密真理，既具压迫感又充满净化力量，需要听众完全臣服于其革命性的音乐逻辑。

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Lucro Sucio; Los Ojos del Vacio' is the unexpected, overly mysterious, and definitely dream-likeninth studio album by The Mars Volta, released in April of 2025 through Clouds Hill, serving as thefollow-up to 2022's self-titled LP and its acoustic follow-up from the following year. The reformedband features an interesting lineup that sees masterminds Omar Rodriguez Lopez and Cedric Bixler-Zavala joined by Omar's brother Marcel, who plays some keyboards and is involved in the engineeringof the album, versatile female drummer Philo Tsoungui, keyboardist-saxophonist Leo Genovese, andbass player Josh Moreau, a session player with some serious experiences in well-known rock andalternative bands. As for the album in question, 'Lucro Sucio' is an 18-track labyrinth of hazy andethereal synth soundscapes, indulgent jazzy interludes, and meditative psychedelic melodies,elevated by the iconic voice of Bixler-Zavala, who sounds as solid as ever on this LP.What I really like about this record is how the gently protruding latin rock elements from the twoprevious albums have been preserved on 'Lucro Sucio', but with an artsy, cryptic undercurrent. Thereis also a very generous interpolation of various synths that allows the pristine production to shinethrough, while the tranquil, ambient tones that prevail give the collection a somewhat ominous, hazyfeel. Leaning more towards trippy art rock than prog, 'Lucro Sucio' is not necessarily the mostsubstantial Mars Volta album, especially when compared to some of the band's intimidating andmaximalist early classics. It almost feels as if Omar and Cedric are attempting to capture theopposite of what their early releases had represented, and to be honest, there is something daringand novel in such a risky experiment. The album is innovative yet accessible, with an abundance ofbeautifully composed electronic-laden psychedelic pieces like 'Reina Tormenta/Enlazan lasTinieblas', 'Cue the Sun/Alba del Orate', 'Poseedora de Mi Sombra', 'Vocifer�', and 'Un Disparo alVac�o'.The finale is a little too monotonous for my taste (that would be last five tracks), but the factthat the entire work weaves through like one continuous piece makes it more diverse and immersivethan the band's 2022 self-titled release. Nevertheless, 'Lucro Sucio' is tame and ethereal, whichfor longtime listeners of the band represents just one side of The Mars Volta's expansive studiosound.
items._genre: art rock / psychedelic / experimental electronic / latin rock / ambient
items._cn_summary: 这是Mars Volta乐队第九张录音室专辑，延续了前作中拉丁摇滚元素，同时加入大量合成器音景与爵士化间奏，整体趋向迷幻氛围艺术摇滚。制作上合成器层次丰富，氛围朦胧而不祥，Bixler-Zavala的人声依然是核心支柱。专辑以18首曲目编织成连续整体，从飘渺电子段落过渡到冥想式旋律，呈现出与早期宏大繁复风格截然相反的克制美学。多首器乐与电子融合段落结构精巧，结尾部分略显单调。整体虽不如早期作品厚重大胆，却展现了乐队主动选择简约抽象方向的实验勇气，对偏好前卫、迷幻、电子融合的听众而言值得深入聆听。

items.body: Her secret lies behind his broken eyes. You carry her all alone inside of you. And you’re still searching for some validation. Why only find frustration? Well, I don’t know. Sometimes the body gets treated like evidence. People inspect it, name it, assign meaning to it, and then act surprised when the person living inside has a different account of who they are. When a person spends enough years absorbing that scrutiny, it can become difficult to tell where somebody else’s judgment ends and their own voice begins. That confusion can be especially brutal for a trans person, because acceptance may require untangling identity from shame that was handed to them before they had the language to reject it. Novelí’s debut single, Mind or Body, begins from inside that argument. The longtime underground DJ, who describes her hybrid of darkwave, synthpop, old-school EBM, Latin freestyle, and related electronic strains as “Maximal Wave,” builds the track from stern machine rhythms, synthetic bass pressure, and melodies that carry the extravagant romanticism of early electronic pop. You can hear traces of Dead or Alive and Depeche Mode in its architecture, alongside the severe physicality of Anhalt EBM and the strange emotional immediacy of a forgotten 1990s game soundtrack playing through cheap speakers in an empty room. Then Novelí opens her mouth. Her register brings Andrew Eldritch and Peter Murphy immediately to mind, though the visual contradiction is part of the pleasure. Novelí embraces femme-fatale glamour while singing in a bass voice she once regarded as incompatible with womanhood. Her own explanation says everything: “I used to think my voice was too deep for a woman, but I’ve grown to think there’s something kind of sickening about being a bass singer who looks like a femme fatale,” Mind or Body gets its emotional voltage through lyrics that move through secrecy, frustration, loneliness, scrutiny, and the weary confusion that comes from being forced to interrogate your own existence over and over. The physical body and social expectation become tangled until even the source of pain becomes hard to locate. Novelí leaves room for uncertainty, but she also introduces a far more dangerous possibility: what if the part of yourself you were taught to hate could become beloved? “Not everyone can relate to the trans experience, but I think almost everyone can relate to feeling like something about you is socially unacceptable, so you feel like you have to carry it alone,” she says. “And ideally, you eventually figure out how to live with it and even embrace it. It’s about entertaining even the tiniest possibility that you can fall in love with the parts of yourself you’ve been hating for a long time.” Daniel Foerste’s accompanying video pushes that idea into religious horror. Novelí appears as a sacrificial figure who eventually becomes a living altar, drawing on Bauhaus, Siouxsie Sioux, Sopor Aeternus, Giallo, Butoh, religious imagery, and vaporwave unreality. “Society sees trans bodies as something horrific, and I wanted to capture that. We’re so often scapegoated, but I also wanted to show that there can be something divine in us, something sacred.” Watch the video for Mind or Body below: Released on the Autumn Equinox and destined for the forthcoming album Transfigure, “Mind or Body” makes transformation feel messy, theatrical, frightening, sensual, and spiritually charged. Novelí has begun her recording career by turning the courtroom inside her head into a nightclub, then placing the accused behind the microphone. Novelí says the sales will support her gender-affirming care and sustain her artistic practice. Listen to Mind or Body below and order the single here. items._cn_summary: 本文介绍跨性别艺术家Novelí的首支单曲《Mind or Body》，她将自身身份探索的经历融入暗潮电子创作，自创风格名为"Maximal Wave"。作品以机械节奏与合成器低音为骨架，融合Dead or Alive与Depeche Mode式的浪漫旋律，以及Anhalt EBM的冷峻质感。Novelí以低音女声演唱，配合femme-fatale式的视觉形象，形成强烈的矛盾张力。歌词围绕秘密、孤独、社会审视与自我认知展开，探讨身体与社会期待之间的纠缠。MV由Daniel Foerste执导，借鉴Bauhaus、Sopor Aeternus与Giallo影像美学，呈现宗教恐怖式的牺牲意象。整体作品在暗潮传统中注入跨性别视角，声音设计与视觉概念均具有鲜明个性。

items.album: John Coltrane 100: John Coltrane in Detroit, June 1966
items.excerpt: John Coltrane Memorial in Hamlet, N.C. Photographer unknown. By Stuart Broomer If I can write anything meaningful about the music of John Coltrane, it may be about the context in which I came to experience his work live, in 1966, after listening intently to his work for four years on record and writing reviews of some of it as well. One’s juvenilia is embarrassing almost by definition, but that’s my particular gateway here to a world in which Coltrane was playing live a few feet in front of me.
items.body: John Coltrane Memorial in Hamlet, N.C. Photographer unknown. By Stuart Broomer If I can write anything meaningful about the music of John Coltrane, it may be about the context in which I came to experience his work live, in 1966, after listening intently to his work for four years on record and writing reviews of some of it as well. One’s juvenilia is embarrassing almost by definition, but that’s my particular gateway here to a world in which Coltrane was playing live a few feet in front of me. 13 months later he passed away. I write this hopefully to communicate something of the challenging world in which Coltrane made his music, that ever more intense, more radically free music, as testimony to his courage and vision as a great artist, as large a person as one might be in that world. The John Coltrane Reference (Routledge, 2008) by Chris DeVito, Yasuhiro Fujioka, Wolf Schmaler and David Wild, edited by Lewis Porter (Routledge, 2008) is a monumental work of scholarship. After the introductions, there’s a Chronology of Coltrane’s life and career that runs to 357 large pages of fine print, followed by a Discography of 404 similarly sized pages in identical print, followed by 49 more pages of appendices, index, etc. Very near the Chronology’s conclusion, there’s an entry for the John Coltrane Quintet’s appearance at Detroit’s Drome Lounge from June 17-26, 1966. The personnel, then consistent, is identified as Coltrane, tenor and soprano saxophones; Pharoah Sanders, tenor saxophone; Alice Coltrane, piano; Jimmy Garrison, bass; Rasheid Ali, drums, Friday to Sunday, matinees on Sunday. Reviewed in Coda (“John Coltrane Quintet – Drome Bar—Detroit” by Stu Broomer, Aug-Sept., 1966, pp.32 - 33). The review is represented by just a few of its sentences, but I’ll restrict myself to the Reference editor’s choices and their punctuation as well. “This is probably the most moving working band in America (…) Tenor saxophonist Farrell “Pharoah” Sanders is now the most important soloist in the group. (…) When (Coltrane) first heard Albert Ayler in 1962, Coltrane told him he had heard himself playing like that in a dream once. (…). This band has recorded five times but nothing has been released. Perhaps Bob Thiele is hoping Coltrane will return to his old-time sanity. I for one hope he will not”. (Reprinted by permission of the author. All Rights Reserved). What I’m trying to get at here about John Coltrane is an essential drive for expression and liberation, for liberation from every constraint to discover what’s real or what’s at least possible. If my memories from 60 years ago mean anything, they’re about the value of revolt and the horror of the norm, the judgmental restriction of cultural norms, in some places becoming more restrictive than anything I might have felt 60 years ago (a festival of liberalism by comparison). As a result, I want the music more intense, more personal, more unpredictable and I’ll stand up for it anywhere. But it is not without ambiguities. As a teenager in the 1960s, I became obsessed with free jazz. It was a promise of freedom from restraint as well as constraint, an explosion of mixed emotions from great sorrow to ecstasy, in effect, perhaps, a promise too far. My absorption in jazz had begun in childhood with the 1957 TV special The Sound of Jazz and followed with the eventual LP. More television: I saw the Robert Herridge Presents episode with Miles Davis and John Coltrane in 1960 and loved it. My brief initial puzzlement and rapid-onset rapture with free jazz started when I picked up the September 1961 Metronome at the corner variety store. It included an epic essay on the jazz avantgarde by the then LeRoi Jones (I still have the essay somewhere — stapled together — the issue is gone). The writing was abstract, mannered and strange but also enchanting (I had already read a paperback of Kerouac’s Tristessa ), its subject an arcane revolution. By the time I had purchased Ornette! and Free Jazz a few months later, Metronome had ceased to exist. I had only Down Beat , a magazine at the time sufficiently reactionary to condemn John Coltrane and Eric Dolphy as anti-jazz in a cover story. A few years later, circa 1965, I started writing for Coda, then Canada’s only jazz magazine. If there’s a shock in that original account (in bowdlerized form), it’s likely the ranking of Sanders’ performance over Coltrane’s. Without digging for the original, I recall moments from that night when I was listening to the dense, tumultuous music and focussing on the brilliant screaming mayhem of the two saxophones, only to open my eyes and discover that John Coltrane was intently hitting a cowbell with a drumstick and Pharoah Sanders was the only person playing a saxophone. This isn’t a criticism of Coltrane. He was one of the greatest musicians who ever played jazz, but we all know now that he was seriously ill and still carrying a heavy musical load. Other memories: I already had certain knowledge that Jimmy Garrison’s solos, as memorably powerful as they were, depended heavily on the bass’s tuning in fourths, and the complex, droning solos dependent to a significant degree on the use of open strings (I was a bass player at the time). At one point in the evening, Coltrane spoke quietly to him (I was sitting at a piano-shaped stage, my ear within four feet of their mouths) specifying the key for one of his extended introductions. Garrison then looked upset, arguing for another key. I wasn’t surprised by the issue. I was surprised that it was happening about four years into Garrison’s tenure in the band. Another and crucial surprise goes to the heart of the history of free jazz. My party (myself and three others, young musicians from Toronto, three Caucasian, one Japanese) were, in effect, insiders (however “out” we might feel in the Drome). We arrived early, conveying Rashied to the venue since we were staying in the same place, the Detroit Artists Workshop. Arriving early, we found a strange mix of conviviality and formality. Standing just inside the foyer, Jimmy Garrison was shaking hands with patrons as they entered. Even to a bass player, Garrison’s right hand (the plucking one) came as a shock: it felt like a bundle of sticks. As popular, as great , as John Coltrane was, there was a fundamental divide in the audience about the shape his music was assuming, that was apparent from the time the music began (a shock perhaps influenced by the very music that Impulse was choosing to release). In essence there were two audiences. In the Drome it happened largely along racial lines, generally slightly older blacks on the one hand, and the white audience, many significantly younger, significantly suspended between hip and hippie. One audience looked disgruntled, offering spare, obligatory applause; the other clapped wildly with exclamatory shouts. Late in the evening, Coltrane broke into the opening phrase of his anthem, “My Favorite Things”, its bright coiling phrases instantly recognizable from the first note. It was amazing. With my back to the rest of the audience, I could actually feel the room lift, so strong was the shift in mood, comparable, for a brief instant, to the sun breaching a cloud cover. Within a couple of minutes, the sonic tumult had taken over again, and one could feel, even more intensely, the mood of the room dropping, to frustration and disappointment, perhaps, and most intensely, I felt, the abandonment, the sense of betrayal. In total, (expanding on Coltrane's grimly disappointed Black audience) the trip seemed at times to be about race but things would get much darker, or should I say lighter (toxic metaphors lurk in our tongue) -- I had gone there with three other young Toronto musicians with whom I played. I had an association with John Sinclair (then in jail on drug charges -- not sure how current John's name is, but his greatest moment of celebrity came when imprisoned during Woodstock: Abby Hoffman interrupted the beginning of the Who's performance with a comment to the effect that Woodstock didn't mean shit while John Sinclair was in jail; then Pete Townsend hit Hoffman with his guitar for trying to take over the Who's stage). In John’s absence, his partner Leni Sinclair was running the Workshop. I knew The Detroit Artists Workshop through shared performances between Detroit and Toronto, performances arranged by John Sinclair and the Toronto poet Victor Coleman of the Bohemian Embassy, a Toronto coffee house and performance space. Shared performances had included members of Detroit trumpeter Charles Moore’s MC5 with featured musicians that had included Marion Brown and Andrew Hill (through which I got to play bass with Andrew for a weekend among other playing associations). I had also published a poem and a record review in John's mimeo'd music journal Changes , which I think may have only gone to two (or maybe three) issues. The Workshop was the epicentre of radical culture in Detroit whether the issue was music, race, drugs, economics or language. Later it was the spawning ground of the MC5, of "Up Against the Wall Motherfucker" fame, who John Sinclair managed. He later was a founder of the White Panther Party, a Black Panther support group. When I met the members of [Ahmed] a few years ago in Guelph, talk turned to Detroit. Some members were thinking about visiting Detroit, and Pat Thomas and I found ourselves reminiscing about John, whose poetry Pat had accompanied during an Amsterdam performance. John's contract, Pat recalled, required a private pot smoking loft. A few days before our group arrived in Detroit, a young inter-racial couple from the Workshop had been violently attacked on the street by the sons of a former Mississippi sheriff whose property adjoined the Workshop at the rear. While we were staying there, the sheriff had invited the residents of the Workshop to a get together/ barbecue to make peace. None of the Workshop residents (naturally) wanted to go and Leni Sinclair asked our Toronto group (whom they were temporarily housing, four males sufficiently groomed to get across the border without close scrutiny) to go as their representatives. We accepted with a certain reluctance, though things (barbecue, blanched pleasantries) went civilly enough. An hour later, on the way out of Detroit, we stopped at an ice cream outlet before we hit the border. The sons and their wives and children were there as well. On neutral ground, none of us acknowledged the existence of the other. Charles Tyler, Stuart Broomer + Perry Robinson, 1966 ©2014 Bill Copeland AN AFTERWORD: 60 years on, I frequently listen to John Coltrane recordings, probably more than to any other historical jazz artist. I have the complete runs of the Prestige and Atlantic recordings and most of the Impulses on CD and the recordings with Monk and Miles Davis and isolated one-offs like Blue Train on Blue Note. My usual listening choices run the gamut from the Prestige and Atlantic recordings (especially Olé , the last of them, with Freddie Hubbard, Eric Dolphy and Art Davis added to the working quartet of McCoy Tyner, Reggie Workman and Elvin Jones). My listening range ends with one of my favorites, Meditations , with the “classic” quartet augmented by Rashied Ali and Pharoah Sanders. I hardly ever, if at all, listen to much that came later. Whether that’s because the actual experience of the last quintet live was enough – sufficiently intense -- to satisfy my need for that music, or that the music is so unstable or destabilizing that I don’t feel a need to hear it in its “frozen” form. The sole exception made among recordings of the last stage is Interstellar Space , the recording of four duets with Rashied Ali, recorded in February 1967, though it too is rarely played, singled out perhaps for the relative coherence of the music and the focus of its intensity. © Stuart Broomer, 2026 Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评围绕1966年6月John Coltrane五重奏在底特律Drome Lounge的演出录音展开，作者Stuart Broomer结合自身亲历现场的记忆与Chris DeVito等人编撰的Coltrane参考著作中的文献，重现了这一历史时刻。文中引用的1966年Coda杂志评论揭示了乐队阵容——Coltrane本人与Pharoah Sanders双萨克斯、Alice Coltrane钢琴、Jimmy Garrison贝斯、Rashied Ali鼓——以及当时乐评界对其激进自由爵士方向的争议。专辑捕捉了Coltrane后期最具实验性的即兴演奏，乐队五人编制释放出高度密集的集体自由能量，音乐朝向更激烈、更个人化、更不可预测的方向发展。这段录音距Coltrane去世仅十三个月，文献与音响共同见证了他作为伟大艺术家在解放与表达驱动下的最后阶段创作。

items.body: Themes and Variations is the first release on Parenthetical Activities, a sub-label of Dissolving which concentrates on experimentation and documentation, recording and amplifying the moments that live ‘in the spaces between the parentheses’. Thomas Shrubsole’s double cassette promises two hours of experimental discourse and intriguing, unrestricted dialogue, is limited to 85 stamped and numbered copies, and includes twelve intuitive acoustic sound-works which are loosely tied together. Recorded over two years, the diverse and eclectic music is written in a nonlinear language of obtuse, curious shapes and fine, angled lines which, as they gel together, create wandering, off-beat sentences and a range of exotic air-hieroglyphics. The dash-dot-dash percussion and the uninhibited, baggy-clothed melody, atypical of dark, late-summer jazz, reclines in the prime time of its intoxicated youth, while quieter interludes, some straddling the borders of total silence, occupy the gaps between music’s accepted and popular lines. Shrubsole invites us to look beyond, to realise that there are no strict beginnings, middles, or endings in music – music is just edited to either begin or fade out at certain points, until the end of its allocated duration. It still sings in the silence; we just can’t pick up its frequencies. Those lines are imaginary, made up because of our inherent need to organise and categorize. The same is true of genres, or the concept of a nation, or the invisible dividing line which separates one country from another; the borders always contested, the soldiers fighting over a plot of land when one side looks just the same as the other. Shrubsole’s audio exploring takes him into no-man’s-land, venturing into the beyond, transcending what we think is possible, breaking barriers and smashing self-conceived and self-restricting borders. They’re ‘studies for alternative instrumental connections’; things that don’t quite fit into the main body of music’s text. Things that live on the outside of the exchange. And the music’s so much richer for its thorough adventuring. This is a mammoth work and a massive undertaking. Altered states are born out of the music’s intricate patterns, and an army of semi-colons, with their brief percussive codes, litter the stave. Shrubsole’s music as Sub Loam has been featured here before, and his approach to music is a freeing thing. For even though the music can at times feel unstructured, the eternal paradox is that there is a structure of sorts, sitting underneath the surface of sound like the lost city of Atlantis. The architecture of the music is submerged, making it trickier to see. Never does it become a gelatinous mess. Boneless patterns appear in less than obvious places, but the soft, swaying drums and the piano’s gentle repetitions and arpeggios reveal the starkly-lit, underground-dwelling structure. It can also be glimpsed in the inner workings of a staccato-blitzed, blip-bleep rhythm. Structure arises out of accidental clashes, out of incidents, out of the creation of music. As soon as Themes and Variations begins to play, the chances of an accidental collision multiply, an accidental returning to structured music when it had initially begun its life with no real predestination. The limited edition comes with two white, stamped cassettes, and a self-locking card box. That box also contains three posters, a twelve-page booklet, and a postcard avec download code. www.parentheticalactivities.blogspot.com
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Parenthetical Activities子厂牌的首发作品，以双卡带形式限量发行85份，收录十二首直觉性的原声实验作品，历时两年录制而成。音乐以非线性语言构建，包含节拍化的打击元素、不羁的旋律线条与晚期爵士氛围，在完全静默的边缘地带安插更安静的间奏段落。创作者试图打破音乐严格的起承转合结构，引领听者进入无人之境——那里没有类型的隔阂，没有国界的争议，只有不断探索的声学连接。鼓点与钢琴的重复与分解和弦在表面看似无序，却暗藏亚特兰蒂斯般沉没的架构。断奏闪烁的节奏信号、柔韧的律动骨架与不显眼的模式共同支撑起丰富的听觉冒险，是一次对声音边界的彻底解放。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德国出生、肯尼亚定居的打击乐手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo组成的二人组Odd Okoddo，邀来83岁肯尼亚东部传统dodo歌唱家Ogoya Nengo共同录制。Kacirek以Buchla合成器、手打击乐与套鼓构建电子律动基底，为两位歌手的人声提供支撑却不喧宾夺主。编曲采用层层叠加策略——合成化多节奏在重复模式中悄然浮现，至曲终已与声音融为一体，仿佛始终潜藏其下。歌曲呈现传统根源与前卫实验之间的张力：老一辈歌手的本土唱腔与电子声响交织，人声在节奏框架内互相抛接，既保留非洲传统深度，又生成面向21世纪的全球化声响。这种将非洲传统声乐与电子实验融合的做法，体现了不同文化在相互回应中既不抹杀传统根基、又使根源本身成为前卫表达的创作路径。

items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由六十年代实验乐队The United States of America主唱Dorothy Moskowitz与意大利作曲家Francesco Paolo Paladino、诗人Luca Chino Ferrari合作完成。十首作品以钢琴为主轴，辅以弦乐、木管与合成器织体，运用相位偏移、模态化旋律与非功能和声等手法，刻意打破听众对西方调性进行的惯性认知。歌词部分延续六十年代抗议歌曲传统，直接触及白人至上主义、威权合谋等政治议题，同时融入对死亡与宇宙的哲学冥思。Moskowitz的演唱不拘泥于旋律线的可预期性，反而以念诵般的意识流方式呈现，让每个词语承载独立重量。整体呈现出实验声响与清醒社会批判并置的特质，适合对非西方音乐叙事与现代政治反思均有兴趣的听众。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家 Omar Sosa 在意大利 Fazioli 钢琴音乐厅完成了一场两小时无脚本独奏即兴录音，素材经后期混入人声采样、打击乐、循环音、田野录音与拾得音效，形成专辑《Sendas》。Sosa 以 Thelonious Monk "绝不重复" 的精神为创作准则，强调首遍即兴的自然性，认为不存在错误音符，并将"少即是多"奉为信条。他拒绝被风格归类，融合爵士、拉丁、古典与世界音乐传统，却刻意回避类型标签。在疫情封锁与个人生活变动的背景下，作品呈现出冥想式的探索气质，开篇曲目通过拨弦与延音进入钢琴共鸣核心，后期叠加轻量打击乐与声效纹理。专辑体现了一位横跨四十年的音乐人对自由即兴与跨文化对话的持续追求。

items._cn_summary: 这张1968年的专辑是Miles Davis在完全转向电声爵士摇滚之前的重要过渡之作。乐评将其与同年发行的《Nefertiti》和《Miles in the Sky》并置比较，认为此作虽在网站评分最低，却是作者个人最爱。专辑延续了Miles标志性的全明星阵容编制，演奏水准精湛。开篇部分强劲有力，随后逐渐转向更为柔和绵密的氛围，整体呈现出一种内敛而诗意的气质。作为后续Bitches Brew时期狂躁电声探索的前奏，专辑在原声爵士与现代爵士之间找到了一个独特的平衡点，调式爵士的框架已开始松动，预示着即兴空间将进一步扩大。

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Soft Machine乐队的首张也是唯一一张由Kevin Ayers担任贝斯手的作品，被视为Canterbury场景的先驱之一。专辑将爵士、摇滚与流行元素融合为一体，尽管部分段落结构复杂、难以跟拍，但精湛的演奏技艺贯穿始终。Kevin Ayers的贝斯与Robert Wyatt的鼓及人声构成了富有律动感的节奏基底，Mike Ratledge的风琴演奏具有催眠般的迷幻特质。乐队成员均为英国人，乐评人强调了那个时代各种新音乐涌现的兴奋背景，以及这张作品在迷幻与前卫摇滚交汇点的开创意义。整体定位虽不完全符合学院派爵士或纯电子/暗潮等核心偏好，但爵士摇滚跨界融合以及对前卫音乐的开创性探索，使其与实验/前卫音乐口味有较高的契合度。

items.body: “Dancing has its time, mourning has its time”, runs a line in “Gamachume”, the new single from Tbilisi artists Tamada and DillaNext, and a Georgian supra works exactly that way. The supra is the country’s traditional banquet, a long table of food and wine presided over by the tamada, who holds the room and proposes toast after toast, to peace, to family, to the homeland and to the dead. The guests drink after each one and often break into song. Singer and producer Lasha Chkhapelia named himself Tamada after that role, and across Dionysus vs Tamada and 2024’s 9 Deadly Sins for Tamada he has written his lyrics as toasts in ancient Georgian and set them over electronic beats. This time the glass is raised to Sukhumi, the main city of Abkhazia, a Georgian region on the Black Sea. Abkhaz separatist forces, backed by Russia, seized the region in the 1992–93 war, and most of the world still recognises it as part of Georgia. Chkhapelia and Zura Jishkariani, the novelist and poet who records as DillaNext, were among around 250,000 Georgians driven out as children. The lyric pictures a boy with a pistol and a rose, with Black Sea currents running down through his genes. The pair used the same image on last year’s “Sokhumeli Bichi” (“Sukhumian Boy”), where the sea ran through the veins of the boy of the title. In both songs the city passes down by blood, from parents who lived there to children who left too young to remember it. Another verse turns a burial into a planting: others dig the earth, he is the one laid in it, and the people who took him for dead find they have planted a tree of life. Thirty-three years after the war emptied Sukhumi of its Georgians, two of the children it drove out are putting the city into songs made in Tbilisi, and that is the tree the verse describes. “Gamachume” arrived with a video on 27 September on Deep Douqan, the label behind Tamada’s most recent singles. It closes on its title, Georgian for “silence me”, five times over, sung by the same voice that earlier claims it can “break armies apart”. At a supra, the tamada decides when the room falls quiet. Stream “Gamachume” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Tamada II DillaNext – GAMACHUME appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Gilla Band Pugnello Dublin rock band deliver their most punishing record to date Pugnello by Gilla Band Have you ever heard a song for the first time and felt a shiver run so deep it took the floor with it? That, for me, is the first seconds of Pugnello, and it hardly relents from there. Dara Kiely comes in screaming on ‘The Angelus’, all scalded shriek, hollering about Bananas in Pyjamas and Gary Lineker as crisp maniac. The track pitches somewhere between Lightning Bolt and a ten-thousand-mile thundercloud, Adam Faulkner’s rolls hurtling underneath like Swans at triple speed. The title rewires the Angelus, RTÉ’s evening bell, into a street preacher bawling in tongues. That opener alone would underline everything they’ve been since France 98... The post Gilla Band – Pugnello appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: Gilla Band 的专辑《Pugnello》以高密度噪音冲击开场，首曲《The Angelus》中主唱 Dara Kiely 以近乎失控的尖叫贯穿，鼓手 Adam Faulkner 的连击滚奏如引擎般驱动整首作品。评论将其与 Lightning Bolt 的原始躁动和加速版 Swans 并置，形容其声响如万雷轰鸣、地面震颤。专辑名本身是对爱尔兰国家广播晚祷钟的一次解构重写，将宗教仪式语汇拖入街头狂啸的语境。整体延续乐队自《France 98》以来的暴力美学路线，在后朋克骨架中注入实验性的声响压迫，是一张倾向于极端聆听体验的独立作品。
